pairs.question: Electrical power is P = V * I. V = 10.0 V with standard uncertainty 0.1 V; I = 2.00 A with standard uncertainty 0.04 A; the two are uncorrelated. Give P and its combined standard uncertainty by the law of propagation of uncertainty.

sources.document: NIST Technical Note 1297 (1994 edition), Guidelines for Evaluating and Expressing the Uncertainty of NIST Measurement Results
sources.locator: Appendix A, A.3, equation (A-3) (law of propagation of uncertainty), with all covariance terms zero

pairs.derivation: dP/dV = I = 2, dP/dI = V = 10. u_c^2 = (2 x 0.1)^2 + (10 x 0.04)^2 = 0.04 + 0.16 = 0.20. u_c = sqrt(0.20) = 0.447213595500 (rounded to 12 significant digits). The reference is the first-order result that the cited equation defines; a Monte Carlo result would differ slightly.

pairs.question: A length is L = x1 + x2. x1 = 50.000 mm with standard uncertainty 0.003 mm; x2 = 30.000 mm with standard uncertainty 0.004 mm; their covariance is 0.000012 mm^2. Give L and its combined standard uncertainty.

sources.document: NIST Technical Note 1297 (1994 edition), Guidelines for Evaluating and Expressing the Uncertainty of NIST Measurement Results
sources.locator: Appendix A, A.3, equation (A-3) (law of propagation of uncertainty), including the covariance term

pairs.derivation: Both sensitivity coefficients are 1. u_c^2 = 0.003^2 + 0.004^2 + 2 x 0.000012 = 0.000009 + 0.000016 + 0.000024 = 0.000049 mm^2, so u_c = 0.007 mm. Ignoring the covariance would give 0.005 mm.

pairs.question: A length difference is d = x1 - x2. x1 = 100.000 mm and x2 = 40.000 mm, each with standard uncertainty 0.005 mm; their covariance is 0.000016 mm^2. Give d and its combined standard uncertainty.

sources.document: NIST Technical Note 1297 (1994 edition), Guidelines for Evaluating and Expressing the Uncertainty of NIST Measurement Results
sources.locator: Appendix A, A.3, equation (A-3) (law of propagation of uncertainty)

pairs.derivation: Sensitivity coefficients are 1 and -1. u_c^2 = 0.005^2 + 0.005^2 - 2 x 0.000016 = 0.000025 + 0.000025 - 0.000032 = 0.000018 mm^2. u_c = sqrt(0.000018) = 0.00424264068712 mm (rounded to 12 significant digits). Ignoring the covariance would give 0.00707 mm.

pairs.question: The area of a square is A = s * s, where s is the measured side. s = 2.000 m with standard uncertainty 0.010 m. Give A and its combined standard uncertainty.

sources.document: NIST Technical Note 1297 (1994 edition), Guidelines for Evaluating and Expressing the Uncertainty of NIST Measurement Results
sources.locator: Appendix A, A.3, equation (A-3) (law of propagation of uncertainty)

pairs.derivation: There is one input quantity, s, so A = s^2 and dA/ds = 2s = 4 m. u_c = 4 x 0.010 = 0.04 m^2. Treating the two factors as two independent measurements would give sqrt(2) x 2 x 0.010 = 0.0283 m^2, which is wrong here because both factors are the same measurement.

pairs.question: A combined standard uncertainty has two independent components, each already multiplied by its sensitivity coefficient: 0.3 mm with 4 degrees of freedom and 0.4 mm with 9 degrees of freedom. Give the effective degrees of freedom by the Welch-Satterthwaite formula, without rounding.

sources.document: NIST Technical Note 1297 (1994 edition), Guidelines for Evaluating and Expressing the Uncertainty of NIST Measurement Results
sources.locator: Appendix B, B.3, equation (B-1) (Welch-Satterthwaite formula). Step 3 says to interpolate or truncate a non-integer result; the reference here is the value before that step

pairs.derivation: u_c^2 = 0.09 + 0.16 = 0.25, so u_c^4 = 0.0625. Denominator: 0.3^4/4 + 0.4^4/9 = 0.002025 + 0.0028444... = 0.0048694... Result: 12.8351397604 (rounded to 12 significant digits). Truncated as the source suggests, this is 12.

pairs.question: A combined standard uncertainty has three independent components, each already multiplied by its sensitivity coefficient: 1.0 mV with 5 degrees of freedom, 2.0 mV with 10 degrees of freedom and 2.0 mV with 20 degrees of freedom. Give the effective degrees of freedom by the Welch-Satterthwaite formula, without rounding.

sources.document: NIST Technical Note 1297 (1994 edition), Guidelines for Evaluating and Expressing the Uncertainty of NIST Measurement Results
sources.locator: Appendix B, B.3, equation (B-1) (Welch-Satterthwaite formula). Step 3 says to interpolate or truncate a non-integer result; the reference here is the value before that step

pairs.derivation: u_c^2 = 1 + 4 + 4 = 9, so u_c^4 = 81. Denominator: 1/5 + 16/10 + 16/20 = 2.6. Result: 81/2.6 = 31.1538461538 (rounded to 12 significant digits). Truncated, this is 31.
